doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Band age, Bob Abrams and bringing his own drums
summary: A joke about the band's old members leads to bassist Bob Abrams and his new upright bass, and why he always brings his own drums.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: And I’m old. Somebody said, “How old is your band.” I said well our band is over 50 years old, and I’m the elderstatesman you might say. I have the second — we’re long in the tooth — I have the second longest set of teeth in the band. He says, “Well who has the longest ones?” “Well” I said, “We have a 75-year-old bassist named Bob Abrams, and he has the longest set of teeth, and with a marvelous set of incisors like that I suppose © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
he’s out somewhere auditioning for the lead role in a Dracula production. You know what a sweet man he is.
He seems to be in a happy time in his life right now and I’m very pleased.
It is and he’s made such tremendous progress on the bass.
And he’s got a real one now too.
I agree. He likes it too now.
It’s a pain to travel around with but you know about that.
You always bring your own drums to this gig, right?

Always. And as a pianist you know how bad it can be if you’re going to a gig and the piano hasn’t been tuned or it’s got a couple of sticking keys. At least when you bring your own drums you know they’re good. So I’m luckier than many pianists.
Yeah, close enough for jazz, I think that’s where the term came from.
